title: Should school days start later?

turns.speaker: Rae
turns.text: The proposal is a ten o'clock start for the sixth form. The biology behind it is apparently quite solid.

turns.speaker: Milo
turns.text: The body clock shifts in adolescence, doesn't it. It isn't laziness.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: It's measurable. Melatonin release moves later by roughly two hours and then drifts back in the twenties.

turns.speaker: Rae
turns.text: So asking a sixteen-year-old to think at half past eight is like asking me to at half past six.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: Roughly, yes. And the districts that moved the start time saw attendance rise and, in a few studies, grades.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: Modest on grades, clearer on attendance and on reported mood. Sleep studies are hard to run well, to be fair.

turns.speaker: Rae
turns.text: The objection is always logistics rather than biology. Buses, siblings, parents' shifts.

turns.speaker: Milo
turns.text: Which are real. A parent leaving at seven can't have a child starting at ten.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: Staggering helps. Primary early, secondary late, which suits both age groups' clocks anyway.

turns.speaker: Rae
turns.text: And the buses run twice, which costs money nobody has.

turns.speaker: Milo
turns.text: There's a sport argument too. Late finish means no training, no part-time job, no evening.

turns.speaker: Cerys
turns.text: That's the trade that actually needs discussing, rather than pretending it's free.

points: A later start for older pupils is proposed on biological grounds.
Adolescent melatonin release shifts about two hours later, returning in the twenties, so early starts conflict with the body clock.
Districts moving start times saw improved attendance and mood, with modest grade effects.
Objections are logistical rather than biological, involving buses, siblings and parents' working hours.
Staggering primary and secondary start times suits both age groups but requires additional transport cost.
Milo notes a later finish reduces time for sport, jobs and evenings, which Cerys says is the trade-off that should be discussed openly.
